title: Chapter 47 — The Mat-Maker
paragraphs: It was a cloudy, sultry afternoon. The seamen were lazily lounging about the decks or gazing vacantly over the rail into the lead-colored waters. Queequeg and I were quietly weaving what is called a sword-mat, to use as an additional lashing for our boat. So still and subdued was the whole scene, and yet somehow so full of anticipation, and such a spell of daydreaming lurked in the air, that each silent sailor seemed dissolved into his own invisible self.

I was the attendant or assistant to Queequeg while he worked at the mat. As I kept passing the filling thread of marline back and forth between the long strands of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads, idly looking off at the water while he carelessly drove each yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess ruled over the ship and the sea, broken only by the intermittent thumping of that great sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself were a shuttle mechanically weaving the unchangeable pattern of my own destiny. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one unchanging vibration, which merely allowed for the crosswise interweaving of other threads. This warp seemed like necessity. And here, thought I, with my own hand I weave my own fate into these unalterable strands. Meanwhile, Queequeg's indifferent sword — sometimes hitting the woof slantingly, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be — and with each weaving creating a corresponding contrast in the final fabric — this savage's sword, thought I, which thus strikes the woof at random, must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity — all three interwoven — none working separately. If chance freely determines the pattern, necessity sets its laws. Free will works somewhere between them. And chance, though limited in its range by both, has the final shaping power over all events.

We were weaving and weaving away when I was startled by a sound so strange, so long-drawn, so musically wild and unearthly, that the ball of free will dropped from my hand, and I stood gazing up at the clouds from which that voice fell like a wing. High aloft in the crosstrees was that mad Gay-Header, Tashtego. His body was reaching eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and at brief, sudden intervals he continued his cries. To be sure, the same sound was perhaps being heard from the mastheads of three other whaling vessels in the same waters at that very moment. But to us, hearing it for the first time, it hardly seemed possible that anything could make such sounds.

As he stood hovering over you, half-suspended in air, peering so wildly and eagerly toward the horizon, you would have thought him some prophet or seer beholding the shadows of Fate, and announcing their coming with those wild cries.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"On the lee beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
The Sperm Whale blows as a clock ticks, with the same unwavering and reliable regularity. And by this the whalemen distinguish this fish from other species of his kind.
"There go flukes!" was now the cry from Tashtego, and the whales disappeared.
Dough-Boy hurried below, glanced at the watch, and reported the exact minute to Ahab.

The ship was now steered away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Tashtego reporting that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bow. For that peculiar trick sometimes used by the Sperm Whale — when, diving with his head in one direction, he nevertheless wheels around underwater and swiftly swims off the opposite way — could not now be at work. There was every reason to believe the whales were heading steadily downwind. And so it proved. Suddenly Tashtego gave a tremendous shout from the masthead.

But at this critical instant a sudden exclamation was heard that drew every eye from the whale. With a start, all stared at dark Ahab, who was surrounded by five dusky phantoms that seemed freshly formed out of thin air.
